verses.text: Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us.
Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.
In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: "My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you.
For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives."
Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father?
If you do not experience discipline like everyone else, then you are illegitimate children and not true sons.
Furthermore, we have all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?
Our fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness.
No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it.
Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees.
Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed.
Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.
See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many.
See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright.
For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.
For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm;
to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken.
For they could not bear what was commanded: "If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned."
The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, "I am trembling with fear."
Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels
in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,
to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?
At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, "Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well."
The words "Once more" signify the removal of what can be shaken—that is, created things—so that the unshakable may remain.
Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe.
"For our God is a consuming fire."

context.author: Unknown. The letter does not name its author. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, and others have been suggested.
context.genre: A sermon in letter form, rich with Old Testament quotations
context.audience: Jewish Christians tempted to go back to old patterns under pressure
context.setting: Surrounded by this cloud of witnesses, the readers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, looking to Jesus. God disciplines those he loves. The writer contrasts the terrifying mountain of Sinai with the heavenly Mount Zion, and warns not to refuse the one who speaks, for our God is a consuming fire.
context.custom: Stadium races were a familiar image, with spectators filling the stands. Esau’s trading of his birthright for a meal (v.16) is a picture of a short-term choice with a lifelong cost. Discipline by a father was a sign of acceptance.
context.timelineBible: Proverbs 3:11-12 is quoted on discipline. Exodus 19-20 describes Sinai with fire and trumpet. Haggai 2:6 is quoted on shaking heaven and earth.
context.sparkNotes: Let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith. Consider him who endured hostility, so that you may not grow weary. The Lord disciplines the one he loves. Strive for peace and holiness. You have not come to a mountain that can be touched, but to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, to innumerable angels, to the assembly of the firstborn, to God the judge, and to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. Since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us offer worship with reverence and awe.

translation.meaning: The one who starts the race and brings it to the finish.
A crowd of people who testify by their lives, like spectators in an arena.

otBackground.note: Quoted in 12:5: "My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord."
I will shake the heavens and the earth.

overview.summary: Run the race looking to Jesus, accept God’s discipline, and remember that believers have come not to Sinai but to the heavenly Zion and an unshakable kingdom.

history.t: Esau sold his birthright for a meal (Genesis 25:29-34) and later found no way to change what he had done, though he sought the blessing with tears (12:16-17).
At Sinai the people begged that no further word be spoken to them (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25), which Hebrews 12:19 recalls.

customs.t: Greek foot races were run in a stadium before crowds. The writer pictures a runner who lays aside every weight, with a "great cloud of witnesses" around him.
The word paideia means the whole upbringing of a child. A Roman father held legal authority over his children, and discipline was a sign that a child was accepted as his own (12:5-11).

archaeology.t: Stadiums have survived at Olympia, Delphi, Ephesus and other cities of the Greek world. Their long, narrow tracks with stone seats on the slopes are the setting the writer's picture of the race would have called to mind.

Today the name Mount Zion is given to the hill southwest of the Old City, where the Dormition Abbey stands. In the Bible Zion usually means the Temple hill or the city of David. In Hebrews 12:22 it means the heavenly city, not a place to visit.

overview.discussion: The writer says to throw off whatever hinders. What “weight” in my life slows me down even though it isn’t exactly sin?
overview.book: The letter to the Hebrews · 13 chapters. A polished sermon showing that Jesus fulfills and surpasses the old covenant.
overview.author: Unknown

historicalImage.caption: The stadium at Ephesus. Footraces in stadiums watched by crowds were familiar across the Greek-speaking world, and Hebrews 12:1 pictures believers running a race with "a great cloud of witnesses" around them.
